name: Constrained decoding and grammar-guided tool calls. Aliases: guided decoding, structured generation, grammar-constrained decoding (GCD), grammar-aligned decoding, logit masking, JSON mode, structured outputs. Implementations: llama.cpp GBNF grammars (GGML BNF, extended BNF with character classes and repetition), Outlines, XGrammar, llguidance (the Rust backend behind Microsoft Guidance), Guidance itself, LMQL, SGLang and vLLM's guided-decoding backends, OpenAI Structured Outputs and Gemini's response-schema mode, Instructor and similar schema-validation wrappers that do post-hoc parsing rather than decoding-time constraint. Key evaluations: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models (Tam et al., arXiv:2408.02442); Generating Structured Outputs from Language Models: Benchmark and Studies / JSONSchemaBench (arXiv:2501.10868); grammar-aligned decoding work on distribution distortion; AdapTrack (arXiv:2510.17376).
kind: Library and inference-engine feature, with an associated body of research results and one benchmark. Not a standard, though JSON Schema and BNF are the formalisms it consumes and OpenAI/Google's structured-output APIs are de-facto interfaces.
maturity: Production and consolidating fast. Grammar constraints are built into llama.cpp, vLLM and SGLang, and are exposed as a first-class API parameter by the major hosted providers, so this is deployed infrastructure rather than a research technique. The performance question that dominated 2023-24 discussion is effectively settled -- the commonly repeated 5-15% overhead figure is obsolete, and current engines report mask computation under 40 microseconds for JSON schemas (XGrammar, roughly 100x faster than earlier libraries) and under 50 microseconds with caching for llguidance-backed Guidance. What is NOT settled is the accuracy question: whether constraining generation degrades the content of what is generated, which remains actively disputed and is the part that matters most here.
license: Permissive throughout and usable here. llama.cpp is MIT and GBNF grammars are part of it. Outlines is Apache-2.0. XGrammar is Apache-2.0. llguidance and Guidance are MIT/Apache-family. vLLM and SGLang are Apache-2.0. The hosted structured-output APIs are service features governed by provider terms rather than licences. For a project running a local GGUF model through llama.cpp, GBNF is available with no additional dependency, which is the practically relevant fact.
keeps_and_discards: Constrained decoding does not read or transform page content -- it shapes the model's OUTPUT. At each decoding step it computes a mask over the vocabulary from the current state of a grammar or schema automaton, sets the logits of tokens that cannot legally continue to negative infinity, and samples from what remains. So it keeps every token sequence the grammar admits and discards every token sequence it does not, with no regard for which the model actually wanted. That last clause is the whole substance of the technique's cost: the discarding is unconditional, so if the model's highest-probability continuation is illegal under the grammar, the model is forced onto a lower-probability path and the resulting distribution is not the model's conditional distribution restricted to the grammar -- it is a greedy per-step approximation of it, which is a materially different object. This is the DISTRIBUTION DISTORTION problem that grammar-ALIGNED decoding research exists to address, and it is the mechanism by which a purely syntactic constraint can change semantic content.
structure_preserved: Perfectly, by construction, in the output: whatever structure the grammar describes is guaranteed present and well formed. A GBNF grammar or JSON Schema is a hard contract, and the output cannot violate it -- there is no parse failure, no truncated brace, no hallucinated field name outside the enum. This is the technique's entire value proposition and it is real: syntactic validity goes to 100% and stays there. What is not guaranteed, and is routinely confused with it, is SEMANTIC correctness -- valid JSON with wrong values, a correctly-typed field containing a fabricated address, an enum value chosen because it was the only legal continuation rather than because it was right. Schema conformance and truth are orthogonal, and the practitioner literature's framing that your JSON is valid but your data is wrong is the accurate summary.
interactive_elements: The direct application here is TOOL CALLS: the model must emit a call naming a function and its arguments, and a grammar can guarantee that the function name is one that exists, that required arguments are present, and that types are right. For this project the specific and valuable case is constraining the model to emit only addresses that EXIST in the trie -- a grammar generated from the current node's child list makes it structurally impossible for the model to request a node that is not there, which converts a whole class of hallucinated-selector failures into an impossibility rather than an error to handle. That is a genuinely strong use and it is the one worth building around.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not applicable to input state, but there is a close analogue on the output side worth naming: a grammar can encode the LEGAL ACTIONS given the current state, so a disabled control cannot be clicked because the action grammar does not admit it, and a collapsed node cannot be read because it is not in the enumerated child set. Encoding state-dependent legality into the grammar is a stronger guarantee than instructing the model about it in the prompt, and it costs nothing at inference time because the mask is computed from the automaton regardless. The cost is elsewhere -- the grammar must be regenerated whenever the legal set changes, which is the delta problem below.
layout_awareness: None. Constrained decoding operates on tokens and grammars; geometry never enters. Fully compatible with no_layout_in_the_fold.
evaluation_method: Two distinct evaluation traditions, and conflating them is the main source of confusion in this area. ENGINE evaluations measure throughput and per-token mask-computation latency on schema suites, typically against a no-constraint baseline on the same serving stack -- this is what the XGrammar, llguidance and vLLM/SGLang comparisons do, and it answers 'what does the constraint cost in time'. COVERAGE evaluations measure what fraction of real-world JSON Schemas an engine can actually compile and enforce, which is what JSONSchemaBench (arXiv:2501.10868) contributes and which turns out to be a real differentiator because JSON Schema has features (recursive references, conditional subschemas, pattern constraints) that grammar backends support unevenly. ACCURACY evaluations measure task performance with and without the constraint, which is what Let Me Speak Freely does across three reasoning tasks and six classification tasks. Only the third answers the question that matters for a design decision, and it is the least often run. The methodological weakness in the accuracy line is that 'constrained' and 'unconstrained' differ in TWO ways -- the decoding constraint and the prompt asking for a format -- and separating the effect of being asked for JSON from the effect of being forced into JSON requires a three-arm design that most studies do not run.
corpus_size_and_origins: Let Me Speak Freely evaluates across three reasoning tasks (arithmetic and multi-hop styles, including GSM8K-type problems, last-letter concatenation and shuffled-object tracking) and six classification tasks (slot filling, intent detection and similar), over several model families -- so its reach is task-diverse and model-diverse but entirely English and entirely benchmark-derived. JSONSchemaBench draws real JSON Schemas from public sources, which gives genuine schema diversity in the thousands, but it measures engine coverage rather than model accuracy. Engine benchmarks use small hand-picked schema sets. Nothing in this literature evaluates on web-derived structured extraction, on tool-call grammars over a live environment, or on anything resembling a trie address space, so every transfer to this project is by analogy. Crucially, nothing evaluates on a 7-8B local model doing multi-step navigation, which is the actual setting.
reported_precision_recall: The decisive numbers, with sourcing and denominators. ACCURACY COST: Let Me Speak Freely reports that format restrictions significantly degrade reasoning capability, that STRICTER constraints produce LARGER drops (a dose-response relationship, which is the strongest form of the evidence), and that the direction reverses by task type -- rigid formats hurt reasoning-heavy tasks such as arithmetic and multi-hop QA and HELP classification tasks such as slot filling and intent detection. The single most useful figure for this project: on function-calling tasks, UNCONSTRAINED generation with post-hoc parsing reached 93.63% accuracy while CONSTRAINED decoding on the same model reached 91.37% -- the always-valid JSON was less accurate than the sometimes-broken JSON, by about 2.3 percentage points. That is a small but real cost, and it is measured on exactly the task class (function calling) that this project would use constraints for. OVERHEAD: mask computation under 40 microseconds for JSON schemas in XGrammar, described as roughly 100x faster than earlier libraries; under 50 microseconds average with caching for Guidance/llguidance; llguidance reported to consistently outperform XGrammar across both vLLM and SGLang in one third-party benchmark. The often-quoted 5-15% throughput overhead is obsolete. VALIDITY: guided decoding raises syntactic correctness to over 96% and as high as 98.2% in one reported RAG-adjacent setting -- note that this is below 100% because the figure blends schema conformance with the harder question of whether the output was usable, and pure grammar constraint gives 100% syntactic conformance by construction. TAKEAWAY: the technique costs microseconds and roughly 2 accuracy points on function calling, buys 100% syntactic validity, and hurts free reasoning more the tighter it is.
independent_oracle: Strong on the syntactic side and weak on the semantic side, and the asymmetry is the whole problem. Syntactic conformance has a perfect independent oracle -- a parser, or a JSON Schema validator, which shares no assumptions with the decoder and gives a definitive yes or no. Semantic correctness has none: nothing checks whether the values are right, and constrained decoding's guarantee is specifically that the artifact will pass the check that CAN be automated, which creates a systematic risk of mistaking the available oracle for the important one. For tool calls over a known address space this project can do better than the literature: constraining to the ENUMERATED CHILD SET means the emitted address is not merely well-formed but REFERENTIALLY VALID, and referential validity is checkable against the store -- which is a genuinely independent semantic check that the general case does not have. That is the strongest argument for grammar-guided navigation here.
evidence_independence: Mixed and the mix is legible. Let Me Speak Freely is academic and independent of the inference-engine authors and of the model vendors it tests, and its finding is unfavourable to the widely-promoted structured-output feature, which raises rather than lowers its credibility. JSONSchemaBench is academic. The overhead figures are largely ENGINE-AUTHOR-REPORTED -- XGrammar's 40-microsecond and 100x-faster claims come from its own authors, Guidance's sub-50-microsecond figure from its own -- and the head-to-head engine comparison quoted above (llguidance outperforming XGrammar on vLLM and SGLang) comes from a third-party inference-optimisation company's technical blog, which is independent of both engines but is a vendor of adjacent services and is not peer-reviewed. Hosted providers' claims about their structured-output modes are self-reported marketing. So: the accuracy costs are independently measured, the speed claims are author-reported and mutually consistent enough to be broadly credible, and the engine rankings should be re-measured locally rather than inherited.
page_archetype_coverage: Not applicable directly. The analogous axis is TASK archetype and it is measured and directional: constraints HELP on classification-shaped tasks (choose one of a fixed set, fill a slot, label an intent) and HURT on reasoning-shaped tasks (multi-step arithmetic, multi-hop inference), with the harm increasing as the constraint tightens. Mapping onto this project's uses: constraining a navigation action -- pick a child address from this enumerated set -- is a classification-shaped task and lands in the regime where constraints help; asking the model to produce a structured summary or an analysis of page content within a rigid schema is a reasoning-shaped task and lands in the regime where they hurt. That split is a clean, evidence-backed design rule and it is the main thing to take from this item.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Under-examined and with one specific mechanical hazard that matters. Grammar constraints operate over TOKENS, not characters, and the mapping from a character-level grammar to a token-level mask is the hard part of every implementation. For scripts whose characters span multiple tokens or whose tokens span multiple characters -- CJK under BPE especially, and any text with combining marks -- the token-level automaton must handle partial-character states correctly, and implementations have historically had bugs here. Practical consequences: a grammar restricting a field to a character class can behave incorrectly on non-ASCII input; a grammar enumerating literal strings (such as a set of child names) must have those strings tokenised consistently with how the model would produce them, and a name containing CJK or emoji may tokenise differently in context. Additionally, forcing a model to emit non-ASCII inside a JSON string interacts with escaping (\uXXXX versus raw UTF-8) and different engines make different choices. All of this is invisible on English test suites. [uncertain] -- these are known implementation hazards rather than measured failure rates; no study located quantifies them.
leaks_outward: Nothing to a page. The relevant disclosure property is inward: a grammar built from the current child list ENCODES part of the store's state into the constraint, which for a locally-run model is harmless and for a hosted model means the schema itself discloses structure (all sibling names, for instance) even before the model generates anything. That is a small but real additional disclosure channel that schema-based APIs create and that is not usually noticed.
mechanism_detectability: Not applicable -- nothing about output constraint is observable to a web page.
countermeasures: Constrained decoding is itself a countermeasure and it is a strong one against a specific class of failure. Against INDIRECT PROMPT INJECTION it provides a real, structural mitigation that no prompt-level defence can match: if the model's output is constrained to a grammar admitting only a fixed action vocabulary with arguments drawn from an enumerated set of existing addresses, then an injection cannot cause the model to emit an arbitrary URL, an arbitrary shell command, or an exfiltration payload, because those token sequences are not in the grammar. The injection can still cause the model to choose the WRONG legal action -- read the attacker's node instead of the one it needed -- so the constraint bounds the damage rather than preventing the influence. This distinction is worth being precise about: grammar constraint reduces the ACTION SPACE available to an attacker to exactly the action space available to the model, which is the correct security property and is far better than filtering. It is the most valuable safety mechanism in this item and it is under-exploited in agent design generally.
measured_fidelity_cost: Measured, and the number is small but not zero: 93.63% unconstrained-with-post-hoc-parsing versus 91.37% constrained on function-calling tasks, i.e. about 2.3 percentage points, against the same model on the same tasks. Read carefully, that comparison also shows the alternative is not free -- unconstrained generation sometimes produces unparseable output, and the 93.63% figure is post-parsing, so the unconstrained arm's failures are simply of a different kind. The broader Let Me Speak Freely finding of a dose-response relationship (tighter constraint, larger drop) means the cost is a design knob rather than a constant: a loose grammar that fixes only the outer envelope costs less than one that dictates every field. Against a control of no format instruction at all, the cost is larger still on reasoning tasks. Nobody has measured this for navigation-style action selection over an enumerated address space, which is the regime this project cares about and which the classification-task evidence suggests should be the favourable case.
determinism: The constraint is fully deterministic -- the mask at each step is a pure function of the grammar and the tokens generated so far, so the SET of legal outputs is exact and reproducible. Sampling within that set remains stochastic unless temperature is zero. This is a genuine reliability gain: the space of possible outputs becomes a decidable, enumerable object that can be reasoned about statically, which is not true of unconstrained generation. The important caveat is the distribution distortion noted above -- constrained sampling is deterministic in its legality and biased in its probabilities, so the OUTPUT DISTRIBUTION is a well-defined but distorted object, and any calibration or confidence read off the model's probabilities under constraint is not comparable to the unconstrained case.
determinism_across_versions: Three drift surfaces. (1) The grammar backend: different engines compile the same JSON Schema differently, support different schema features, and handle token-boundary edge cases differently, so the same schema can admit different outputs on vLLM's XGrammar path versus llama.cpp's GBNF path -- these are not interchangeable and a schema validated against one is not guaranteed on the other. (2) The tokeniser: a grammar's token-level mask is derived from the model's vocabulary, so changing the model changes the compiled automaton even for an identical grammar, and a grammar tuned around one tokeniser's quirks may misbehave on another. (3) The schema dialect: JSON Schema has multiple drafts with incompatible semantics, and engine support varies by draft. Practical rule: pin the engine, the model and the schema dialect together, and treat a grammar as validated only for that triple. GBNF has an advantage here for a llama.cpp-based project -- it is a single format in a single implementation with no dialect question.
reproducibility: High relative to everything else in this research set. A grammar is a small text artifact, the engines are open source, and the constraint's behaviour is a decidable property of the grammar and the vocabulary. Storing the grammar alongside the output makes any generated artifact's legal space re-derivable years later, which is a real reproducibility property that unconstrained prompting does not have. The irreproducible part remains the model, as everywhere.
failure_modes: (1) VALID BUT WRONG -- the dominant real-world failure; the schema is satisfied and the values are fabricated, and the validator cannot tell. (2) FORCED CONTINUATION -- the model's preferred token is illegal, so it is pushed onto a low-probability path and the output diverges semantically from what it would have said; this is the distribution-distortion mechanism and it is how a purely syntactic constraint damages content. (3) REASONING SUPPRESSION -- a tight schema leaves no room for intermediate reasoning, and since the model cannot think in tokens it is not allowed to emit, reasoning-heavy tasks degrade; this is the mechanism behind Let Me Speak Freely's dose-response finding and it is why 'thinking before constraining' designs exist. (4) SCHEMA UNSUPPORTED -- the engine silently ignores or rejects schema features it cannot compile (recursive refs, conditionals, patterns), so the guarantee is weaker than the schema states; JSONSchemaBench exists because this is common. (5) INFINITE OR DEGENERATE GENERATION -- a grammar admitting unbounded repetition lets the model loop until the token limit, producing valid, useless, expensive output; a grammar with an unreachable state can deadlock generation. (6) TOKEN-BOUNDARY BUGS on non-ASCII content. (7) GRAMMAR STALENESS -- a grammar generated from a page state that has since changed constrains the model to actions that no longer exist, which is a correctness failure specific to a live environment and is not discussed in this literature at all.
failure_visibility: Split in an unusual and mostly favourable way. Syntactic failure becomes IMPOSSIBLE rather than invisible, which is the strongest form of loud-failure engineering available -- the class of error is eliminated, not detected. Schema-feature-unsupported failures are silent in some engines and loud in others, and should be tested for explicitly at grammar-compile time rather than trusted. Semantic failures are entirely silent and are made MORE dangerous by the constraint, because a well-formed output carries an unearned appearance of correctness and downstream code stops validating. The design response is to keep validating semantics after the parse, and specifically to check referential validity -- does this address exist, does this action apply to this node's current state -- rather than treating schema conformance as sufficient. Grammar staleness is silent and needs an explicit generation-counter check.
scale_limits: Cost is per decoded token and is now small: sub-40-microsecond mask computation for JSON schemas, sub-50 with caching. The costs that DO scale badly are elsewhere. GRAMMAR COMPILATION is the expensive step -- building the token-level automaton from a grammar is orders of magnitude more expensive than applying it, so a grammar that changes on every request pays compilation every time and can dominate. That is precisely the regime a dynamically-generated child-list grammar falls into, and it is the main engineering hazard for the use proposed here. Engines cache compiled grammars keyed by the grammar text, so the mitigation is to make the grammar STABLE and put the variability in the data -- constrain to a generic 'address' shape and validate referential existence after parsing, rather than enumerating the current children as literal alternatives in the grammar. That trades a hard guarantee for a soft check and is the correct trade whenever the child list changes frequently; the enumerated form is right when it is stable. Vocabulary size also matters: the mask is over the whole vocabulary at every step, so very large vocabularies raise the constant.
delta_cost_model: The technique has a clean per-token cost and the delta question is about the GRAMMAR, not the tokens. Applying a compiled grammar is O(1) per token in the size of the address space; compiling one is not. What falls OUTSIDE a per-change cost, stated so the interaction with an O(delta) design is falsifiable: (1) GRAMMAR RECOMPILATION whenever the legal action set changes -- if the grammar enumerates the current node's children, then every DOM mutation that adds or removes a child invalidates the compiled automaton, so a delta of one node costs a full grammar compilation, and on a live page that is a serious amplification; (2) the compilation itself is superlinear in the number of enumerated alternatives for some backends, so a node with a thousand children produces an expensive grammar; (3) caching keyed on grammar text means any change produces a cache miss, so there is no partial reuse -- grammars do not compose incrementally in current engines; (4) the mask is over the full vocabulary every step regardless of how constrained the state is, so cost is insensitive to how much the constraint actually restricts. The design consequence is direct and worth stating as a rule: DO NOT put rapidly-changing state into the grammar. Constrain the SHAPE of an action (verb, address syntax, argument types) with a stable grammar compiled once, and enforce the CONTENT (does this address exist right now) by validating the parsed result against the trie, which is an O(depth) lookup and is exact. That keeps the hard syntactic guarantee, keeps a hard referential guarantee, and keeps grammar compilation off the delta path entirely.
reanchoring_stability: Not an anchoring mechanism. Adjacent point: a constrained action grammar can require the model to emit an address in a canonical form, which eliminates a whole class of malformed-selector problems and makes every emitted reference directly resolvable against the store -- so constraint improves the reliability of the re-anchoring INPUT even though it does nothing about re-anchoring itself.
adversarial_exposure: The most valuable safety property in this item, and it deserves to be stated precisely because it is often overstated. Constrained decoding provides a STRUCTURAL bound on what an injection can make the model DO: if the output grammar admits only {expand(address), read(address), act(address, verb)} with addresses in a canonical form, then no amount of injected text can produce an arbitrary URL fetch, a data-exfiltration string, a shell command or a call to a tool that is not in the grammar -- those outputs are not merely discouraged, they are unreachable. This is categorically stronger than prompt-level defences, which ask the model not to comply, and it composes with them. What it does NOT do: it cannot prevent the injection from influencing WHICH legal action is chosen, so an attacker can still steer navigation, cause the model to read attacker-controlled content preferentially, or induce a wrong-but-legal action. And it cannot prevent exfiltration through a legal channel -- if any grammar-admitted field is free text that later reaches the network, that field is an exfiltration path, so free-text fields in an action grammar should be treated as the security-critical part and either eliminated or bounded. The practical rule: make every argument an enumerated or referentially-checked value wherever possible, and audit any free-text field in the action grammar as a potential covert channel. Note also the interaction with item 30: constrained decoding restricts output, not input, so it does nothing about the model being persuaded -- it only limits what the persuasion can cash out as.
provenance_carrying: The grammar can REQUIRE provenance, which is a mechanism worth using: making an address field mandatory in every output structure means the model cannot produce an unattributed claim, because an output without the field is not grammatically valid. That turns 'please cite your sources' from an instruction the model may ignore into a structural impossibility, and it composes directly with the citation-based failure detector recommended in item 30. This is one of the few places where a hard guarantee is available for a property that is otherwise only ever requested politely, and it is a strong argument for grammar-constrained output in this project even setting aside the tool-call case.
roundtrip_safety: Guaranteed on the syntactic axis: constrained output parses by construction, so generate-parse is a fixed point for structure and the escaping is handled by the grammar (a JSON grammar cannot emit an unescaped quote inside a string). This eliminates the escaping hazards that afflict every free-text structured emission, including the markdown-injection class. The remaining round-trip question is semantic and is not addressed: parse-then-re-serialise will reproduce the same structure with the same wrong values.
token_budget_and_ordering: Two effects, pulling in opposite directions. FAVOURABLE: a constrained output is minimal by construction -- no preamble, no apology, no explanatory prose -- which cuts output tokens substantially and makes cost predictable, and predictability matters more than the absolute saving when the output feeds a loop. UNFAVOURABLE and better documented: a schema that leaves no room for intermediate reasoning suppresses it, and Let Me Speak Freely's dose-response finding means the tighter the format the worse the reasoning. The resolution the literature converges on is to SEPARATE the phases -- let the model reason in free text first, then constrain only the final action or structured payload, which is what 'thinking before constraining' designs do and what a two-field schema (a free reasoning field followed by a constrained action field, in that order) achieves in one pass. Ordering within the schema matters and interacts with item 30's findings: the reasoning field must come BEFORE the constrained answer field, because the model cannot condition on tokens it has not yet emitted, so a schema that puts the answer first has structurally prevented the reasoning from informing it. That is a concrete schema-design rule that is easy to get wrong and that costs accuracy silently.
representation_cost: Negligible in inference time (tens of microseconds per token) and negative in output tokens (constrained outputs are shorter). The real cost is the accuracy delta -- about 2.3 percentage points on function calling, larger on reasoning-heavy tasks, favourable on classification-shaped tasks -- and the engineering cost of grammar compilation and maintenance. What is lost per token saved: the model's ability to reason in the output channel, which is why the free-reasoning-then-constrained-action pattern is the right shape rather than a compromise.
what_could_be_adopted: Five things, in order of value. (1) A STABLE ACTION GRAMMAR for the model's tool-call surface -- a fixed set of verbs with canonically-shaped address arguments, compiled once. This gives 100% syntactic validity, eliminates hallucinated selectors and malformed calls, and provides the structural injection bound described above, at a cost of tens of microseconds per token. It is the single most valuable adoption in this item. (2) REFERENTIAL VALIDATION AFTER PARSING rather than enumeration inside the grammar, so that grammar compilation stays off the delta path while the guarantee that an address exists is still hard -- an O(depth) trie lookup. This is the specific engineering resolution of the grammar-staleness and recompilation problem and it is not something the literature offers, because the literature does not consider live environments. (3) MANDATORY PROVENANCE FIELDS in the output schema, making unattributed output grammatically impossible. (4) THE FREE-REASONING-THEN-CONSTRAINED-ACTION SCHEMA SHAPE, with the reasoning field ordered first, which recovers most of the reasoning cost that Let Me Speak Freely measures. (5) GBNF SPECIFICALLY for a llama.cpp-hosted local model, since it is in-tree, has no dialect ambiguity, and avoids the JSON Schema feature-coverage problem entirely. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: dynamically enumerating the current child list as grammar alternatives on every step, which puts recompilation on the delta path; tight schemas around content-analysis or summarisation output, which is the regime where constraints demonstrably hurt; and any assumption that schema conformance implies correctness.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. A grammar constrains the model's OUTPUT format and makes no claim about the page's structure; it names no region, classifies nothing, and encodes no heuristic about what page content means. The one thing to watch is that an action vocabulary must stay generic (expand, read, act on an address) rather than growing site- or region-specific verbs, which would smuggle structural assumptions into the interface. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS; no geometry anywhere. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS PROVIDED THE GRAMMAR IS STABLE, WITH A NAMED EXCEPTION IF IT IS NOT. Mask application is O(1) per token and does not scale with the store. Grammar COMPILATION is expensive and does not compose incrementally -- no current engine supports partial recompilation, and caching is keyed on exact grammar text -- so any design that regenerates the grammar per page state pays a full compilation per delta, which is a genuine and easily-overlooked O(delta) violation. The recommended split (stable grammar for shape, trie lookup for referential validity) removes it. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- the constraint runs in the real inference path against the real model and there is no stub temptation; if anything it strengthens the no-mocks position by removing the need for output-parsing fallbacks that are themselves a form of silent degradation. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO INTERACTION. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is, and it is the strongest available structural defence against indirect prompt injection in this whole research set -- it bounds what an injection can cash out as, rather than trying to detect it. The measured accuracy cost is real but small (about 2.3 points on function calling) and is largely recoverable by putting a free-reasoning field ahead of the constrained action field. The one adoption error to avoid is putting page-derived, rapidly-changing state inside the grammar.
governance_signal_handling: None; this is an inference-time mechanism with no retrieval component. One indirect and useful application: a fetch action's URL argument could be constrained to a grammar of permitted origins, making a governance decision (this origin's signals permit access) structurally enforceable rather than advisory -- an origin the policy forbids simply is not emittable. That is a genuinely novel use of the mechanism and it is the only place in this research set where a governance rule can be made unbypassable by the model rather than merely instructed.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not a data-processing mechanism. Two second-order points. First, constrained output is minimal output, so less content is generated and retained, which is mildly favourable for minimisation. Second and more usefully, a grammar can be used to PREVENT the model from emitting certain content classes into stored artifacts -- for example by making free-text fields absent from the schema entirely, so that page content cannot be copied verbatim into the model's output and thence into a log, which is a hard rather than advisory control over what ends up retained. That is worth considering for any output path whose results are persisted. [uncertain] on the specific analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject.
